activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The flyer went up on Monday morning outside the cafeteria: club sweatshirts, eighteen dollars each, and Peyton, who as treasurer of the junior class had argued for the price in a meeting she now wished she could forget, stood in front of it with her backpack sliding off one shoulder. Eighteen dollars was what the senior class had charged last year, and last year the seniors had sold forty-two. So far this week the juniors had sold nine.

"Lower it," said Marcus, who was class president and had wanted twelve dollars from the start. He was eating a bag of chips at the bench behind her, and the cafeteria noise around them undulated as third period let out, a wave of voices rising and breaking against the walls. "Twelve dollars, sell more, done."

"That's not how it works," Peyton said, though she was not entirely sure how it worked, which was the problem. "If we sell more at twelve but make less per shirt, we could still lose money. There has to be a middle somewhere."

Marcus crumpled the chip bag and tossed it toward the recycling can, missing. "So find the middle. You're the one taking calculus."

She had walked into fifth period already annoyed, because being told to use calculus was like being told to use a language she had been studying for exactly six weeks. On the board, Ms. Rojas had written a function, then its derivative, then a number line with plus signs to the left of a point and minus signs to the right, and Peyton had copied it without feeling anything land. She understood the algebra. What she did not understand was why anyone cared which way the signs pointed, and Ms. Rojas, who was cheerful to the point of being choleric in reverse, had a habit of saying "you'll see" that Peyton found less than comforting. Today's quiz had a problem exactly like the board work, and Peyton had gotten it right, she thought, but the rightness felt borrowed, like wearing someone else's coat.

After school she went looking for her grandfather, who was already in his usual spot in the corner of the family center, where he sat on Tuesdays waiting for her while her mother finished her shift. He had driven a delivery truck for thirty-one years and done the dispatch math in his head, and he was the only person Peyton knew who thought numbers were something you could argue with. When she laid out the sweatshirt problem, the nine sold, the seniors' forty-two, the deadline on Friday, he pulled a napkin from the dispenser and smoothed it flat with the side of his hand.

"Suppose we pretend people buy fewer shirts every time the price goes up," he said. "Some steady drop. What's that called in your class?"

"A linear model," Peyton said. "If it drops off at a constant rate." She wrote revenue equals price times the number sold, and below it she substituted what she actually wanted: price times some starting quantity minus a rate times the price, all of it multiplied out into a polynomial, an x squared with a negative coefficient out front. Then she took the derivative the way Ms. Rojas had drilled them, the power rule falling out of her pencil almost without her deciding anything.

"Those signs again," her grandfather said, tapping the derivative she'd set beside a rough number line she'd drawn to test it.

"It's the first derivative test," Peyton said, mostly to hear whether the words still belonged to someone else. She marked a plus sign to the left of the critical point and a minus sign to the right, and then she stopped, because she saw it: where the signs went from positive to negative, the function had to be rising and then falling, which meant that point was a local maximum. Not a guess for the middle. The actual top of the hill, at least as far as the model went. She checked the arithmetic twice and got fifteen dollars, and under it, a revenue that beat both eighteen and twelve by a margin she made herself recalculate a third time before she would say it out loud.

"Of course," her grandfather said, "people aren't a formula."

"I know." And she did know, which was the part she couldn't put on the napkin. Maybe the drop-off wasn't steady. Maybe eighteen dollars worked as a disincentive for freshmen in a way it wasn't for seniors with jobs, or maybe this year's juniors were just slower to buy and the nine would become thirty by Friday regardless of anything she did. The model said fifteen; the world might say otherwise. She folded the napkin into her pocket anyway.

At Thursday's meeting she put the napkin, unfolded and flattened, in the middle of the table, and Marcus leaned over it with his arms crossed. "You're telling me the answer's fifteen."

"I'm telling you the model says fifteen," Peyton said. "We can test it. One day, one price, and if it's wrong, we'll know the model's wrong, not just me." Marcus looked at the napkin for a long moment, then at the sign chart with its plus and minus, and pulled out his phone to change the flyer.

By Friday afternoon they had sold eleven more, and Peyton stood by the cash box counting singles, watching the line of students at the table stretch past the water fountain and wondering whether to trust the number in her notebook or the evidence of her own eyes, and deciding, for now, to hold both.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search works only on sorted data: it compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half of the list that cannot contain it.
story:
Jade had agreed to debug Rohan's code over the phone, which turned out to mean listening to him panic while she sat on her grandmother's porch with a glass of sweet tea going warm beside her. The club's new membership roster had two hundred and six names in it, and their little program was supposed to find any one of them. It kept coming back with nothing found, even for names everyone knew were in there, like Okafor, which was the whole reason the program existed.

"It's a binary search," Rohan said, as though saying it again would make it work. "I read about it last night. It's supposed to be faster than checking every single name one at a time."

"Than a linear search," Jade said, mostly to show she'd been listening. She didn't actually know yet what made the two different, beyond a vague sense that one was a plodder and the other was supposed to be clever. That was the embarrassing part. She'd told the club she could fix it. She'd said it in the confident voice she used when she hadn't yet looked at the problem, a voice she was starting to suspect she used to externalize an optimism she didn't really hold.

Her grandmother came out with the newspaper folded under her arm and settled into the other rocker. She had been a county clerk for thirty-one years and regarded computers the way she regarded weather, as something that happened to other people. "Who are you arguing with?" she asked.

"Nobody. A program. It keeps missing names that are definitely there."

Her grandmother made a small sound, the sound of a woman who had filed a great many things. "Come inside when you're done shouting. I'll show you something."

What she showed Jade was the old phone book she still kept in the drawer by the refrigerator, because she didn't trust the internet to be up when she needed it. "You city children search like this," she said, and turned to the front of the book, and ran her finger down the first page, one name at a time, mouthing them. "Aardvark Removal. Abel. Abelard." She glanced up. "How long do you think I'd be at it before I reach Whitfield?"

"Forever."

"Now." She opened the book wide, found the exact middle, and put her finger there. "I look at the name in the middle and I think, is the name I want before this or after it?" Her finger rested on a name somewhere around Morgan. "Whitfield comes after. So I take the front half and I throw it away." She let the pages flop forward, half the book gone in one motion, and Jade felt something rearrange itself in her head. "Then I find the middle of what's left and do it again. Whitfield. After. Throw away the front half. Two hundred pages, then a hundred, then fifty."

"It works because it's sorted," Jade said slowly. "Because the names are in order, you know which half can't have it."

Her grandmother shrugged. "I'd be a fool to throw away half the book if I didn't know what order it was in."

Jade was already dialing. "Rohan. Is the roster sorted?"

There was a silence long enough to hold a whole confession. "Sorted how?"

"Alphabetically, Rohan. Is it alphabetical." She could hear him scrolling. The club had entered members in the order they paid dues, which was the order they'd walked into the gym on sign-up day, which was the order of nothing at all. The list was two hundred and six names of pure chronological accident, and Rohan's program had been cheerfully discarding the half that contained Okafor every single time, because a binary search on unsorted data was just a machine that threw away the right answer with great efficiency.

She stayed three more days at her grandmother's, and each morning she sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, sorting the roster and rewriting the search with a note tacked to the top of her screen in her own handwriting: check the middle, then throw away the half that can't hold the target. It felt strange to be learning the cleverest thing she knew from a woman who called the laptop "the television with keys," but there was something fitting in it too. Her grandmother had spent three decades believing that how you organized information was a moral question, that an unsorted file was a small act of chaos, and Jade had spent the summer believing the opposite, that structure was something the machine would supply on its own. She wasn't sure yet how to hold both ideas, whether her grandmother's whole ontology of careful record-keeping and her own faith in fast code were rivals or just two halves of one job. The club members back home, disaffected after weeks of a search tool that couldn't find their own names, would take some winning back either way.

On the last evening she ran the finished program. She typed Okafor and hit enter and the result appeared in less time than it took her to exhale. Her grandmother looked over her shoulder at the glowing screen and rocked back on her heels.

"Faster than reading every name," Jade said.

"Of course it is," her grandmother said. "Now close that thing and help me shell these peas."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
The blood pressure cuff hissed and Aiden watched the needle settle on the dial, one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four, which meant nothing to him yet. Marisol, his partner in the health aide track at Camp Wanocksett, unwound the cuff from his arm and wrote the numbers on her clipboard with an air of ceremony, as if the gesture itself were the skill. Their instructor had given them a handbook, a box of practice cuffs, and almost no direction, saying only that by Friday each of them had to take a reading, interpret it, and explain it aloud to the group. Aiden flipped through the handbook that evening on the dock, the lake going copper behind him, and found a page he had skimmed past the first time. Under the 2017 American guideline, it said, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.

He read the line three times, then set the book on his knees and looked at the water. His grandfather had mailed him a photograph last month, before camp started: the little log the old man kept beside his armchair, columns of numbers in his careful draftsman's handwriting, taken every morning with the home monitor Aunt Renata had insisted on. Grandpa had written something insouciant on the back, "Still alive, see you in August," which was his way of refusing to take any of it seriously. Aiden had looked at the numbers then and felt only a vague unease, the kind you get from a receipt you can't quite read. Now he pulled the photo up on his phone, zoomed until the columns blurred, and found the entry from the second week of June: 136 over 85.

There was a kid at camp named Derek who wore a stethoscope around his neck between sessions, which everyone agreed was an affectation, since they were nowhere near the simulation where stethoscopes were actually issued. Derek had done a first aid certification the year before and liked to hold court at the picnic tables. "Stage one hypertension," he announced the next morning, when Aiden mentioned what he'd found in the handbook, tapping his own neck where the stethoscope hung. "That's what those numbers are called. My mom's a nurse." Aiden asked him what a person was supposed to do about it, and Derek shrugged, said something about salt, and drifted off toward the boathouse, apparently satisfied to have named the thing without ever wondering what the naming was for.

Aiden wasn't satisfied. He carried the question through the afternoon like a stone in his shoe. During free swim he sat on the dock again with Marisol, who was teaching herself to interpret readings by inventing patients. "This one," she said, pointing at a made-up 148 over 92, "that's past your range, right? So that's stage two, or worse." She said it lightly, burnishing her own competence a little, but she was the only one taking the arithmetic seriously, and Aiden found he trusted her more than Derek for exactly that reason. He showed her his grandfather's log. She went quiet over it, scrolling, then said, "He wrote you this and didn't take it to anybody?"

"I don't think he looked at it that way," Aiden said. "He thinks of it like checking the oil. Numbers in a notebook, job done." He was remembering now the summer he was twelve, when Grandpa had ignored a splinter in his palm until the whole hand swelled, and Grandma had driven him to the clinic herself, furious, while Aiden sat in the back seat watching the fields go by. She had died the following spring. There was no one left to do the driving now, and no one left to be furious, which Aiden understood, in a way he couldn't articulate, was the actual problem.

Marisol said, "So call him." It was that simple for her, and he envied the simplicity. He thought about it through dinner, through the evening campfire, through the walk back to his cabin under a sky gone loud with cicadas. If he called and said the words, stage 1 hypertension, his grandfather would hear a lecture, would hear Aunt Renata, would go amiable and dismissive and promise to mention it at some appointment he would not schedule. If he said nothing, the log would keep filling up with numbers in that steady hand, and Aiden would carry the June entry around like a folded map to a place he'd never been.

The next morning was interpretation day. When his turn came, Aiden took Marisol's reading, one hundred and twenty-six over seventy-eight, and stood in front of the group and worked through it aloud, systolic and diastolic, below 130 and below 80, within the normal range under the 2017 American guideline, not hypertension, not even stage one. He heard his own voice steady on the terms, and he heard, underneath it, the sentence he was not saying to anyone. Derek, mercifully, kept quiet. The instructor marked something on her clipboard and called the next pair up.

That night Aiden walked out past the flagpole to where the camp's one payphone hung on the wall of the mess hall, a relic nobody used. He fed in the quarters he'd been carrying since Monday and dialed the number he knew by heart. It rang twice, three times, and he watched a moth circle the bare bulb above the phone while he decided, one more ring at a time, exactly what he was going to say. Then his grandfather's voice came on the line, cheerful and unhurried, and said, "Well, this is a surprise."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The lab smelled like chalk dust and the faint vinegar of old agar, and Jessica had copied the same DNA sequence onto her worksheet three times before she trusted her hand. Mr. Reyes had left a strand on the board, AGCTTAG, and told them to write the RNA it would produce. She wrote it out letter by letter, then checked it against her notes, then sat back with the particular hollowness that comes from realizing you do not know how to check something you have just done.

"You're stuck too?" Devon leaned over from the next stool, holding his pencil like a dart.

"I'm not stuck. I'm thinking."

"Same thing in this class." He was being facetious, but only halfway, the way people are when the joke is a shelter. "I got TCGAATC for mine, but I don't know if that's RNA or just DNA wearing a costume."

Jessica looked at his paper. At the bottom, in his cramped left-handed scrawl, he had written TCGAATC and then, in the margin, the word RNA with a question mark after it. She looked at her own answer. AGCUUAC. She had copied the strand faithfully, flipped the letters to their partners, and there, sitting in the middle of the third position, was a T. She had put it there herself, five minutes earlier, without noticing.

"Wait," she said.

"That's encouraging."

"No, really. Look." She turned her worksheet so he could see it. "In the DNA, adenine goes with thymine and guanine goes with cytosine. That part I know cold, I made flashcards in September. But when you write the RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. So adenine still pairs with adenine's partner, but it's U, not T. There shouldn't be any T in mine at all."

Devon squinted at her paper, then at his own. "So I've got two problems."

"You've got at least two problems." She took his pencil out of his hand and crossed out the second letter. "If the DNA you started with had adenine there, you write U."

"You're sure?"

She was not sure. That was the thing she could feel pressing at her from underneath the certainty of her voice: she had said it with confidence because saying it with confidence was how you found out whether you believed it. The rule felt right, the way a key feels right before you turn it. She pulled her binder toward her and found the page from the unit on RNA, the diagram with the two strands and the letters floating between them, and there it was in the print, the same pairing she had just said, the U standing where she expected a T.

"Okay," she said. "Okay, it's right."

"You didn't know?"

"I knew it the way you know someone's phone number. You have to say it out loud before you know if it's in there."

Down the row, Priya was erasing something with such force that her whole worksheet buckled. Jessica watched her do it, then watched her write the same wrong letter again. Priya was the one who had explained mitosis to the whole table last month, drawing circles on the desk with a wet finger, and Jessica had privately considered her the standard, the person whose understanding indemnified the rest of them against their own confusion. It had never occurred to her that Priya could also sit in this room at 2:15 on a Tuesday with an answer she could not defend.

"Hey," Jessica said, not loudly. "Check your T's."

Priya looked up. "What?"

"In your RNA. If you were copying from DNA, adenine pairs with thymine in the DNA itself, but in RNA it's uracil instead of thymine. If you've got T's in there, they came over from the DNA side."

Priya looked down at her paper for a long moment. "I have four of them."

"I had one. It's like the T is a stowaway."

The three of them worked through their sequences together after that, calling out letters, arguing briefly about whether guanine went with cytosine or the other way around, which was an argument that resolved itself the moment they realized it was symmetrical and therefore not an argument. Devon kept saying that if he had to choose, he would rather be graded on the DNA, since at least DNA kept its letters in one place, and Jessica told him that was exactly backwards, that the copying was the point, the whole reason any of it counted as a mechanism rather than a word game. Language, her philosophy teacher had said that morning, works because the sign stays put while the meaning moves. Here the letters had to move so the meaning could stay. She did not say this out loud. She thought it and then, because thinking it felt like showboating, she let it go and wrote U where U belonged.

The bell rang while Priya was still recopying her sequence, and Mr. Reyes came down the row collecting worksheets without looking at them, which meant the checking would happen later, elsewhere, by someone they would never see. Jessica handed hers over with the corner folded where she had pressed too hard.

"Read the board on your way out," Reyes said. "Homework's changed."

She looked. The assignment now read: explain, in one paragraph, what you would tell someone who insisted RNA and DNA were the same molecule. Devon groaned beside her.

"Great," he said. "Now we have to explain the thing we just barely stopped getting wrong."

"We're the experts," Jessica said, and swung her bag over her shoulder. "We know exactly which mistakes get made."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
story:
The paycheque lay flat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of unfinished cereal, and Ashton read it the way other people read the fine print on lottery tickets, which was to say suspiciously and from top to bottom. He had worked sixty-two hours over three weeks at Marconi's, the Italian place on Dundas where he bussed tables and refilled water glasses until his wrist ached, and the number at the top of the stub said $744. The number at the bottom said $623.51. He set the paper down, picked it up, and read it again.

"Mom," he said. "They took over a hundred dollars."

His mother was at the other end of the table with her own paperwork, a shoebox of receipts and a laptop she treated like a hostage negotiation, opening one tab at a time. "That's income tax," she said without looking up. "Federal and provincial. And there's CPP and EI on there too, probably." She had her own want this evening, which was to finish her tax return before midnight, because last year she'd filed late and the delay had eaten a month of her refund, and the refund was going to fix the dryer that had started making a sound like a dying accordion.

Ashton pulled the stub closer. The deductions were itemized in a font so small it seemed designed to discourage exactly the scrutiny he was giving it. Federal tax, provincial tax, Canada Pension Plan, Employment Insurance. Each line was only a few dollars or a few dozen, but together they had quietly subtracted $120.49 from what he'd understood to be his. He was saving for a used keyboard, a Yamaha someone in his building was selling for $600, and he had been counting his hours times his wage in his head all month, which now struck him as a kind of pleasant fiction.

"There's more of it everywhere," his mother said, almost cheerful about it, and slid a restaurant receipt across the table. It was from the dinner she and Ashton had grabbed after his shift on Friday, pasta for her, pizza for him. "Look at the bottom."

He looked. Total before tax, $34.50. Then a single line, HST, $4.49. Then total, $38.99. He frowned at it, because he'd expected two lines. He'd seen American receipts online, in the group chats where people argued about prices, and those had separate lines for state tax and whatever else. This one had only one.

"It's the Harmonized Sales Tax," his mother said, peering at it briefly. "Ontario combines the federal GST with the provincial sales tax into one thirteen percent line." She tapped the receipt with one finger, a gesture that closed the subject as far as she was concerned, and returned to her shoebox.

Ashton did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope, because there was a satisfaction in doing it by hand that he couldn't have explained and didn't try to. Thirteen percent of $34.50 was $4.485, which rounded to $4.49. One line, one rate, no split. So when he'd been telling his friend Deshawn that everything in this city cost some secret extra amount on top of the sticker price, he'd been right in a way, but wrong in the shape of it. It wasn't hidden and it wasn't layered. It was sitting there in the open, one line, thirteen percent, added to nearly everything he bought, which meant it was added to the keyboard too. Six hundred dollars was actually six hundred and seventy-eight. He sat back in the chair and stared at the ceiling, mesmerized less by the number than by the realization that the whole economy was speaking a language he had been hearing his entire life without translating.

"The return's asking if I want to answer all these questions about climate incentives," his mother muttered. "It's so prolix. Paragraph after paragraph for a checkbox."

"Then don't read it," Ashton said.

"I have to read it. If I check the wrong box I get a letter in April and then I panic until June." She rubbed her eyes. "Do yours."

"Mine?"

"You worked. You paid tax on income. You file a return." She turned the laptop toward him. "You probably get most of it back, you made almost nothing."

He had planned to watch videos and go to bed. Instead he pulled the laptop across the table, and for the next forty minutes the two of them worked in parallel, the shoebox slowly emptying on her side, his T4 slip, which he'd folded into his back pocket and sat on for a week, smoothed flat on his. The form asked him things he didn't know the answers to at first, and then, line by line, he found he did know them, because the answers were on the paycheque stub he had already interrogated. Income here, tax already paid there. The form subtracted one from the other in front of him.

He was halfway through when he stopped and reread the line about tuition credits and then a line about the disability amount for his mother, which he'd never considered, and a thought surfaced slowly, the way water moves through an aquifer, unseen and under pressure, arriving at a well nobody drilled on purpose. All month he'd been thinking of tax as a thing that was done to him, a subtraction, a hand in his pocket. But the return was running the arithmetic backwards, and the backwards arithmetic ended in his favour. He'd been counting his wages wrong the whole time, in both directions. The sticker price of the keyboard was bigger than the sticker. His paycheque was smaller than his pay. And the system that took from him in April gave some of it back in spring, or was supposed to, if you filled in the boxes and didn't panic until June.

"Eighty-one dollars," he said finally, leaning back.

"Refund?"

"Refund." He looked at the number on the screen, then at the paycheque stub, then out the dark window toward the building across the lot where the Yamaha waited in somebody's basement. Six hundred and seventy-eight with the tax. He had $520 saved, plus the eighty-one coming, plus two more shifts this week. His mother submitted her own return a few minutes later, closed the laptop with ceremony, and announced that the dryer was going to live.

"I thought this stuff was going to be boring," Ashton said, stacking his envelope, his stub and the receipt into a pile and squaring the edges against the table.

"It is boring," his mother said. "That's not the same as useless." She stood, then paused with her hand on the back of her chair. "What's the keyboard cost again?"

"Six seventy-eight," he said. "One tax line. I checked."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The branch on Carling Avenue had a shelf of deposit slips, a bowl of stale mints, and a desk at the back where Landon sat every Tuesday and Thursday after school, opening mail for the assistant manager and shredding what she told him to shred. He had taken the placement through his school's co-op program because his mother said a bank would look better on a university application than the grocery store, though the work itself mostly involved a letter opener. On the Thursday in question he had spread two leases across the desk beside the shredder, and he was reading them for the third time.

The first lease was for a one-bedroom above a hardware store on Bank Street. Rent was fourteen hundred a month, and the tenant paid electricity and heat separately. The second was a basement unit near Lansdowne, fifteen hundred and sixty, with heat included but electricity and water billed to the tenant. His friend Dev wanted him to decide by Saturday, because Dev's cousin had already offered to drive the boxes.

"Those aren't bank documents," said Mrs. Okonjo, passing with a stack of cheques.

"They're mine," Landon said. "Sort of. Mine and Dev's."

She looked at the pages for a moment, said "carry on," and continued toward the vault.

Landon made a column on the back of an envelope. He wrote the fourteen hundred, then underneath it the words hydro, heat, water, each with a blank. The landlord above the hardware store had sent him a note saying the one-year term would begin June first and that they should come in Friday to sign. There was something in the landlord's tone, a briskness, that made Landon feel the deadline was firmer than it probably was. His grandfather would have called the tone a peccadillo, a small fault hardly worth naming, and would have said so while reaching for a coffee.

His grandfather did in fact arrive at eleven, as he did most Thursdays, to deposit the proceeds of a small business repairing violins. He was a compact man who wore the same grey jacket in all seasons and who regarded the bank as a place one visited with the same regularity as a barbershop. He took a number even though Landon was visibly alone at the desk.

"Grandpa," Landon said, "do you know anything about leases?"

"I know mine." His grandfather lowered himself into the chair across the desk. "Twelve years in the same apartment on Byron. The term ended years ago and I never signed another thing."

"You never signed? Aren't you, like, squatting?"

"I'm a tenant, not a squatter. In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month on the same terms, automatically." He said it the way he said most things, as though reporting the weather.

Landon wrote this down on the envelope, under the column of blanks. "So the landlord can't just kick you out for not signing?"

"I said it continues. Don't add to what I said."

Mrs. Okonjo called a number, and a woman with a stroller went forward. Landon looked at the hardware store lease again. Section 4 gave the term as one year, beginning June first. If the term simply ended and the tenancy carried on, then the pressure he had felt about Friday was not pressure at all, or was pressure of a different kind, the kind that worked only on people who hadn't asked. He did not say this aloud, because saying it aloud would have transmuted a hunch into a plan, and he wasn't sure yet it was a plan.

"Which one are you leaning toward?" his grandfather asked, nodding at the pages.

"I don't know. The cheaper one isn't cheaper if the utilities are huge, and I can't find out what the utilities are without living there."

"Estimate."

"That's not knowing."

"Nothing is knowing. You repair a crack in a violin belly knowing the wood will move anyway. You still glue it."

His number was called. He stood, buttoned the grey jacket, and added, "Bring the numbers to Sunday dinner. Your aunt moved apartments four times; she made every mistake available." Then he went to the counter and counted out his cheques.

Landon spent his lunch break at the desk with the envelope. He found an old hydro bill in his email from his mother's house and scaled it for one bedroom instead of four: maybe sixty a month for electricity. Heat was harder, since the hardware store unit had baseboard heaters and the basement was partly underground. He called the utility from the branch phone, and a recorded voice gave him an average winter cost for a similar unit, which he wrote down and then rounded up, because averages were made of people who had survived. Water, the city website said, ran about forty. He added the column twice. The Bank Street unit came to roughly sixteen eighty a month all in. The basement, even with heat included, came to about the same, within twenty dollars either way, depending on a winter he could not predict.

The margin was so small that the choice stopped being about money and became about the lease terms themselves, and about which landlord had tried to make him feel a deadline that the law did not require him to feel. That was a reason, but it was not a clean one, and he could admit that his own certainty had shifted twice since morning, once when his grandfather spoke and once when the numbers came out even. Some things would stay uncertain: the winter, the neighbours, whether Dev would actually help carry boxes. He folded the two leases together, put them in his backpack, and left the envelope with the arithmetic on it squared on the desk.

On his way out he passed the phones for sale on the wall by the door. He called the hardware store landlord, and a man answered on the second ring.

"I have a question about the lease," Landon said. "If the year ends and we don't sign a new one, it just continues, right? Month to month?"

There was a pause long enough that Landon could hear someone in the background asking about a delivery.

"That's right," the man said. "It continues."

"Okay," Landon said. "Then we'll come look at the place Saturday, and I'll bring a calculator."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
The festival smelled of fried dough and cardamom, and Arianna kept one hand on her phone in her pocket like something she was guarding from her mother. She had told her, twice on the drive over, that she had already checked the academic calendar, that Eid would fall safely after finals, that there was no conflict at all. This was true in the sense that she had thought about checking it very hard while lying on her bed the night before.

"Smile at least," her mother said, handing her a paper plate of kebab. "People will think you're here under arrest."

"I'm smiling."

"You're displaying the general arrangement of a smile."

Her little brother Sami had already disappeared toward the henna tables, and her father stood near the stage with the other uncles, arguing happily about something that would end in someone buying everyone tea. Arianna took a bite and felt the torpid weight of the whole school year settling over her, the exams that began Monday, the history outline she had not written. She had counted on June. Eid had been in June last year, blazing and easy, the whole block closed off for the parade, and she had assumed, the way you assume the tide stays where you left it, that it would stay.

Her phone buzzed. She turned her shoulder away from her mother.

From Nadia: ok don't panic but the exam schedule came out. Your history final is Tuesday morning. From Nadia: which is Eid. From Nadia: I'm sorry. I know you said it moved after exams.

She read it three times. Around her, children were chasing each other between the folding tables, and a man at the sound system was testing the microphone, and nothing about the festival had changed at all except that it had happened in the wrong season, arriving like a guest who keeps earlier appointments every year.

Her mother was watching her, though, so Arianna typed back: I'll email the teacher tonight. There's a policy for religious observance. It'll be fine. She put the phone away. She was not going to ruin her mother's one good day this month over a scheduling problem she had created herself, because that was the part she was beginning to admit: nobody had moved Eid. Eid moved. Someone at the volunteer booth, an older girl she half knew from the mosque, had said it casually last summer, that the calendar ran on the moon and came ten or eleven days earlier every year, so Ramadan would slide backward through spring and then winter before anyone noticed. Arianna had nodded and filed it nowhere. If she had filed it, she would have known June was never coming back.

Her mother took the empty plate from her. "You have that face."

"What face."

"The one you had at nine years old when you broke the vase and rearranged the shelf to hide it."

"I don't have a face," Arianna said. "I have a situation."

Her mother walked with her to the edge of the festival, past the banner strung between two lampposts, past the aesthete uncle who was photographing the lanterns from six angles and complaining that the string lights had been hung without any sense of rhythm. At the curb, the noise dropped away and they could hear traffic again, the ordinary city going about its Saturday.

"Tell me," her mother said.

"History final is Tuesday morning. It's Eid. There's a form I can file for religious accommodation, but I have to do it Monday, and I have to actually study this weekend, which is this weekend, meaning now." She heard her own voice compress everything into logistics, delimiting the problem neatly so it wouldn't spill into anything larger. "And I told you it wasn't a conflict. I told you I'd checked. I didn't check. I decided it."

Her mother was quiet for a moment. Down the block, Sami came running with a smeared henna design on his palm, shouting that he'd gotten a lion, and it looked more like a duck, and their father was laughing somewhere behind him.

"So file the form," her mother said. "And study tomorrow, and study Sunday, and Tuesday morning you take the exam and Tuesday afternoon you eat like a horse. You think this is the first time Eid landed somewhere inconvenient? Ask your grandmother about fasting through final exams in Karachi. Ask her about fasting in July." She straightened Arianna's collar, a small unnecessary adjustment. "You're not in trouble with me. You might be in trouble with the registrar, but the registrar doesn't make kheer."

"I'm sorry I lied," Arianna said. "Sort of lied."

"Sort of is the only way anyone lies," her mother said, and started walking back toward the music.

Arianna stayed on the curb a moment longer and opened her email, thumbing out a draft to the history teacher, requesting the accommodation form, deleting the apology, putting it back in. Behind her the microphone crackled to life and someone began the call to gather everyone for the afternoon prayer, the old words rising over the bunting and the paper lanterns, and she pressed send.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
Kaitlyn had claimed the window seat before anyone else was awake, which was the only way to get it, and she had fortified her position with a mug of tea, two pillows, a hiking magazine open to a photo of montane wildflowers she was ignoring, and the battered copy of Huckleberry Finn that her book club had assigned for Sunday. She had read forty pages last night, laughing in a way that embarrassed her, and now she was trying to figure out why.

The problem was that she was supposed to lead the discussion. Priya had texted her a list of questions, and the second one was "Who's telling this story, and can we trust him?" Kaitlyn had underlined it twice and then underlined a passage where Huck describes Jim planning to buy his wife back and then steal his children if their owners would not sell them, and Huck says it "most busted the meeting," that it was enough to make a body ashamed of the human race. She had stopped underlining after that, because her pen hovered and her thoughts stalled. Huck was reporting honestly. That much she felt sure of. And yet every instinct she had said he was wrong, deeply wrong, about what he was seeing.

Her brother Dev wandered through with his calculus homework and colonized the corner of the window seat, because treaties meant nothing to him. "Can you check this?" he asked. "We're supposed to parametrize the curve, you know, write x and y in terms of t." She glanced at it, said his t should be squared, and watched him actually listen, which was rare. Then he saw her book. "Oh, Huck Finn. We read that in ninth grade. Everyone laughed at the part where he describes the circus and thinks the drunk performer is really in danger."

"Did you?" she said. "Why did everyone laugh?"

"Because the performer is a trained acrobat pretending to be drunk, obviously. Huck is panicking, he thinks the man is about to die, and the whole audience is in on it except him." Dev went back to his parametrization. "It's funnier because Huck doesn't get the joke."

Kaitlyn sat very still with her mug going cold in her hands. That was it, or near it. Huck reported the circus honestly, every detail, and still misunderstood the whole thing, so the reader saw the acrobat while Huck saw a doomed drunk, and the laughter came out of that gap between them. The same thing was happening with Jim, only there was nothing to laugh at. She pulled the magazine toward her, flipped past the wildflowers, and wrote in the margin of a page torn from her notebook: he tells the truth and misses the meaning. Underneath she added, we see more than he does. It was the closest thing to a thesis she had, and it fit both the circus and the shame.

Priya and Marcus arrived Sunday afternoon with a bag of chips and Marcus's little sister Nia, who could not be left at home and who installed herself under the window seat like a cat. Priya had prepared, in her way, which meant she had read the spark notes and half the book and formed three strong opinions. "The narration is the whole book," she announced. "That's my thesis."

"That's not a thesis, that's a genre," said Marcus.

"It's a thesis if I defend it." Priya stole a chip. "Okay, Kaitlyn, you're leading. Start us off."

Kaitlyn read the circus scene aloud, and everyone laughed, even Nia from under the seat, who could not possibly have followed it. Then she read Huck's line about Jim's plans for his children, and the laughing stopped with an almost audible click. She waited. Marcus looked at his shoes. Priya put the chip bag down.

"So here's what I think," Kaitlyn said. "He's a naive narrator. That's the term, I looked it up. He reports everything honestly and misunderstands almost all of it, and we're always seeing one more layer than he is."

"Which is why the funny scenes work," Marcus said slowly. "The joke is real to us and invisible to him. He's the only person in the whole book who doesn't get it."

"And the terrible scenes work the same way," Priya said, quieter now. "He thinks he's doing wrong by helping Jim, and we can see he's doing right. His conscience is on the wrong side, and he reports that honestly too." She frowned at the window. "So do we trust him or not?"

"That's the part I can't settle," Kaitlyn admitted. "I trust him to tell me what happened. I don't trust him to tell me what it means. And I keep flipping between those two like they're one question when they're really two."

Nia's head emerged from under the seat, holding a hiking magazine she had been quietly shredding, the montane wildflowers now confetti in her fist. There was a silence in which everyone calculated the damage.

"Reparations," said Marcus solemnly. "That magazine deserves reparations."

"Add it to the list," Priya said, "right after whatever we owe Mark Twain," and she held out the chips so Nia could shake on it.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
Keira found her grandmother's recipe card propped against the flour canister like it had been waiting for her, which, in a house where nothing waited, felt almost deliberate. The card read Lemon Cake, Do Not Double in her grandfather's cramped handwriting, and below that, in her grandmother's looser script, a phone number crossed out and rewritten twice. Keira had come to make it because her mother had emailed last week: "Your grandfather's birthday is Saturday and I can't get there. Someone should bake his cake. He pretends he doesn't care, but he does." The email had ended with a reminder to monetize her babysitting hours wisely if she wanted spending money for the fall, and Keira had rolled her eyes at her phone, but she had also bought lemons.

The kitchen smelled of the rosemary her grandmother grew on the sill, though her grandmother herself was at physical therapy, which was why the house was quiet enough to hear the refrigerator hum. Keira set the card where she could see it, washed her hands, and began. She creamed the butter and sugar until they turned pale, cracked in the lemon zest, sifted flour and baking powder together with a patience that surprised her. Her grandfather shuffled in around then, ostensibly for coffee, and stood at the counter pretending to read the back of the newspaper.

"You're halfway to something," he observed.

"Lemon cake. Don't look at the recipe, you'll spoil it."

"I wrote the recipe."

"Then don't look at it from memory."

He laughed, a dry sound, and settled onto the stool by the window. He was not, Keira thought, a man easily described as sanguine; he worried about the gutters, about her college applications, about a spot on his arm the dermatologist had declared harmless twice. But today he seemed almost relaxed, watching her, and she found herself performing small competences for his benefit, leveling the flour with the back of a knife the way her grandmother did.

She was folding the dry ingredients into the butter when she reached the line that said two eggs, beaten. She opened the refrigerator with the confidence of someone who had not checked, and the egg shelf held a jar of pickled beets, half an onion wrapped in plastic, and a carton of egg substitute her grandmother used for omelets, expired in March. Keira stood there holding the door and doing arithmetic: the cake was wet and leavened and halfway combined, her grandfather could not drive at dusk, the nearest store was a twenty-minute walk, and butter plus flour plus sugar left to sit would not wait for her.

"Problem," she said.

"Out of eggs?"

"How did you know?"

"Your grandmother's been clearing the fridge. Happenstance, probably. She never plans to be out of anything, but she is." He folded the newspaper with the air of a man delivering a verdict. "There's a hen next door. Mrs. Aldous. She trades for tomatoes."

Keira looked at her bowl, then at the clock, then at the sliding door to the yard. "The batter can't just sit."

"No," her grandfather agreed. "It cannot."

She went out through the garden in her apron, still dusted with flour, and knocked on Mrs. Aldous's screen door. The old woman came slowly, drying her hands, and listened to the whole story with her head tilted.

"Lemon cake," she said. "Bernard's birthday?"

"Saturday. I'm doing it today because everyone's coming tomorrow." Keira hesitated, then said the true thing. "I didn't check the eggs first. I just started."

Mrs. Aldous nodded as though this were a confession she heard weekly. "You know what cooks call it, setting everything out before you begin? Measuring, preparing, all of it in place first? Mise en place. My mother said it meant you never get caught halfway." She turned toward her kitchen. "Sit down, I'll get you three. Take three, in case one's bad."

Keira carried the eggs back across the frost-bitten yard cupped in her apron like something that might hatch, and found her grandfather had not moved from the window, though he had turned the oven on for her without being asked. The batter took the eggs and rose in the pan, and the kitchen filled with the smell of lemon and browning butter. When the cake came out, domed and golden, Keira set it on the rack and pulled her phone from her apron pocket.

She typed to her mother: "No eggs at halfway. Grandpa's neighbor bailed me out. Learned the hard way about mise en place." Then she looked at her grandfather, who was already reaching for the serrated knife he kept for the first slice of anything, and she deleted the last sentence, and typed instead: "Cake's done. Come Saturday if you can."

He cut two slices before it had even cooled.

"For quality control," he said. "Get me a fork."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United States has no national sales tax; sales taxes are set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depends on where the purchase is made.
story:
The envelope had to be at the county clerk's office by four o'clock, and at three fifteen Evan was still standing in line at the bank with two paycheque stubs, a birthday card from his grandmother containing forty dollars in cash, and a folding table of receipts balanced in his mind like a waiter's tray. His father was in the parking lot with the engine running. The deposit had to clear today, because the fee for the community college payment plan was drafted on the first of the month, and the first of the month was tomorrow.

The line moved slowly enough that Evan could read his stubs a second time. He had started work at the hardware store in June, and every two weeks the stub told him the same quiet story in smaller numbers than he expected. His gross pay was 472 dollars, but the net, the part that actually landed in his account, was 396.40. Somewhere in that seventy-five-dollar gap lived a federal income tax withholding, a state income tax withholding, and something called FICA, which the stub listed without apology. He had asked his father about it once and gotten a shrug that meant, approximately, welcome to being a person.

"You can come up now, hon," said the teller, a woman named Dolores according to the placard on the counter. Evan slid the cheque and the deposit slip under the glass. His hands were sweating, which embarrassed him, so he pretended to organize the receipts instead. Dolores stamped something, and the stamp made a small decisive sound, like a door closing.

"My dad says I should save every receipt," he said, mostly to fill the silence. "For taxes. I don't know what he thinks I'm going to deduct."

"It doesn't hurt," Dolores said. "Though sales tax on snacks won't save you."

Here was the thing that had been bothering him since Tuesday. On the drive back from his grandmother's, he and his friend Priya had stopped for gas in one town and then, fifteen minutes later, for iced tea in the next town over. Same brand of tea, same size, nearly the same shelf. In the first town the receipt showed 2.19 plus eleven cents of tax. In the second, the same drink rang up with nine cents of tax. Priya had gotten obstreperous about it, tapping both receipts on the dashboard and declaring that somebody was being cheated, and Evan had not known what to tell her. He still didn't. He had a folder in his backpack with both receipts paper-clipped together, like evidence in a case no one would adjudicate.

"There's no national sales tax," Dolores said, counting his forty dollars into the drawer. "It's the states and the local governments that set it. So the rate depends on where you buy the thing."

"So the tea in Fairview was taxed at a different rate than the tea in Dayton."

"Two different places, two different rates. That's how it works."

Evan stood there while she printed his receipt, holding both halves of something in his head. On one side was his father's voice, which tended toward the view that any tax was a kind of slow robbery administered by an oligarchy that had never fixed a pothole in its life. On the other side was Priya, who thought taxes were what adults paid instead of being decent on purpose, and that complaining about them was itself a little embarrassing. Both of them had evidence. His stub showed a real seventy-five dollars leaving him every two weeks, money he had earned carrying bags of concrete. And the road had shown him two towns, fifteen minutes apart, quietly disagreeing about what a bottle of tea should cost at the register, neither of them obviously wicked.

He did not land anywhere final. That was the honest part. It seemed to him that the withholding on his stub bought something, though he could not name what, and that the eleven cents versus the nine cents were both small and both real, and that a person could hold all of that at once without picking a team. He wrote to Priya about it that night, after the envelope had been stamped and mailed with forty minutes to spare. His note said: "The tea wasn't a scam. There is no national sales tax in this country, so the rate depends on where you buy it. I checked. But I still think the paycheque thing is worth being angry about, a little. Are you coming Saturday?" He sealed it, printed his own name under hers on the envelope, and left it on the kitchen table weighted with a jar of nails.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
Chloe had failed the first quiz, a 58 circled in red pen, and tomorrow was the retake, so she spread her notes across the kitchen table and tried to say it out loud: DNA gets copied, the copy gets read, the reading becomes a protein. Saying it was the problem. On paper the words arranged themselves into neat arrows, DNA to RNA to protein, but when she opened her mouth the arrows collapsed.

Her brother Danny sat at the other end of the table stringing beads for a craft project, sorted by color into little dishes like eggs in a carton. He was twelve and mercurial, sulking over a lost soccer game an hour ago and now humming. Their cat, long habituated to the noise of the household, slept through everything on the windowsill above the sink. Near the cat lay a thick envelope their mother had left on the counter before driving back to the office, a subpoena, she'd said at dinner, something for a case she couldn't discuss, and the word had hung over the meal like weather.

"Can I use you?" Chloe asked.

"For what?"

"I have to explain this stuff to someone who doesn't know it. If I can explain it to you, I actually know it."

Danny shrugged, which meant yes. Chloe picked up her pencil and held it like a microphone, then felt stupid and put it down.

"Okay. So the cell needs to make a protein. A protein is a chain, like a chain of beads. But the instructions are locked in the nucleus, in the DNA, and the protein gets built outside, in the cytoplasm. So first the cell makes a copy of the gene. That's transcription. The copy is called messenger RNA."

"Messenger," Danny said. "Like a delivery guy."

"Sort of. It carries the instructions out. Then the copy gets read, and that part is translation, and that's where I get lost, because there's this machine."

She looked at her notes. The diagram showed a lumpy gray blob on a wavy line, with little labeled triangles sprouting off it. TRNA. Codon. Ribosome. She'd memorized the labels for the quiz and still couldn't make a sentence that meant anything.

"Wait," Danny said. He held up his necklace, a cord with seven beads on it. "I'm doing this. I read the pattern card and I add the bead it says, one at a time, and the string moves through my fingers. Watch." He slid a green bead down the cord, then an orange one, consulting a strip of paper where he'd written the order in colored dots. "The card doesn't become the necklace. I read it and I build the necklace."

Chloe stared at him. In her diagram the gray blob sat on the wavy line, and the wavy line was the messenger RNA, the copy, and the blob moved along it. Not the other way around. The reader moved along the message.

"The ribosome," she said slowly. "The ribosome is your hand. It moves along the messenger RNA, reading it, and it picks up amino acids, those are the beads, and it joins them together to build the protein chain."

"Okay."

"And the way it joins them, the connection between the beads, that has a name. Peptide bonds. The ribosome links the amino acids with peptide bonds." She said it twice more under her breath, testing whether it held its shape. It did.

Danny slid another bead onto the cord and frowned at his pattern card. "What if the card gets smudged? Like if one dot is wrong?"

"That would be a mutation. One wrong bead in the whole necklace."

"Could be bad or nothing."

"Yeah." She wrote it on the margin of her notes: ribosome = hand moving along string, reading pattern, joining beads. She wondered whether her teacher would think the comparison was too simple, whether the real thing, the actual cell, would resist being turned into a boy with a craft project. Probably it did resist. Probably there was more, and the diagram was already lying to her by leaving things out. But it was a lying she could correct later. Tomorrow she needed a sentence she could stand behind.

Later that evening, after their mother came home and put the subpoena in a drawer, after Danny abandoned the necklace half-finished on the table, Danny lay in bed listening to Chloe through the wall. She was talking to herself again, the low murmur he'd grown up falling asleep to. He caught the words peptide bonds, twice, then ribosome moves along, then a pause. He thought about his half-necklace downstairs, seven beads and a pattern card, and how she'd looked at him like he'd said something important when he'd only been showing off. He didn't understand what the words meant, exactly. But he understood the tone, the same tone she used practicing her college interview answers, the tone of someone rehearsing a future.

In the kitchen, on the table, the necklace lay in a stripe of streetlight. Chloe came down for water at midnight, saw it, and picked up the cord. She held it the way Danny had, thumb and finger, and moved her hand slowly along the empty string past the beads, mouthing something to no one, then set it down exactly where it had been and carried her glass upstairs.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and the oranges somebody's mother had already started slicing. Natalie carried the folding table in with Deshawn, and they set it against the far wall under the scoreboard, which still showed the final from Tuesday: 58, 61, a loss that had ended the season and, for the five seniors, everything else. Coach Okafor had given them the keys and gone home. She had said only, "Lock up when you leave."

Natalie was a junior, a sixth man, and she had planned the party the way she planned everything, with a list taped inside her locker: music, table, water, trash bags, a banner that said GOOD LUCK SENIORS in paint that had bled through onto the cafeteria floor beneath it. What the list had not planned for was Priya crying in the corner by the ball rack, or Marcus standing at half court shooting free throws in street shoes, one after another, missing most of them.

"Rylie's not coming," Deshawn said. "Her mom texted me. She said she can't." Rylie was a senior, a point guard, the one who had taught Natalie the crossover in July. Natalie looked at the door, then at the banner, and started folding the paint-stained banner smaller, as though putting it away sooner would fix something.

"Should we wait?" she asked.

"We're here. She knows we're here."

The seniors drifted in anyway, the ones who came: Priya, drying her face with the hem of her warmup shirt; Marcus, still shooting; a girl named Beth who had been hurt all season and had kept score at every game anyway. They ate orange slices and stood in a loose circle at the top of the key, and nobody sat down, and nobody left, and the circle held like something that could not decide which it wanted to do.

From there, from inside the circle, Beth watched Natalie take out her phone. Natalie had a psychology elective, third period, and she had spent that afternoon's dead time scrolling her notes, and now she held the phone up and read aloud, her voice flat from the gym's echo: "In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate."

"That's the whole thing?" Marcus said.

"There's diagrams. Forming, storming, norming, performing, and then adjourning." Natalie turned the phone so they could see the chart, five boxes in a row. "They wrote the first four in 1965. The fifth one came after."

Beth had heard of the first four, sort of, from some training her mother had done for work. She had not heard of the fifth. She watched Priya read the word with her lips moving, adjourning, like she was tasting it, and Beth understood the taste before Priya said anything, because Beth was the one who had been hurt, the one standing outside the huddles all winter, keeping the book, and she had known all along that the team was a thing that would end and that its ending had no substitute. She just had not known it had a name.

"So we're in it," Priya said. "Right now. Stage five."

"We're not, though," Natalie said. She was still holding the phone, and Beth noticed she had turned it off without seeming to realize it, screen dark, thumb over the button. "Rylie's not here. If this is the stage, we're doing it wrong, or we're doing a partial one, or it's not the same because she's at home and we're here."

"You think everyone has to be standing in the gym for it to count?"

"I think it's a chart," Natalie said. "I think charts are what people make after, to explain what already happened. I don't know what we're in."

Marcus banked his last free throw in, softly, off the square, and the net made its small sound. He walked over and looked at the dark phone in Natalie's hand, then at the circle of orange peels on the floor by the table. He had a scholarship to a school two states away, and Beth had heard him tell Coach in the parking lot that the remuneration was the only reason he was going, that he would have stayed home otherwise, and she had thought at the time that it was a strange word for money and an honest one for what a school buys when it buys you.

"Call her," Marcus said.

Natalie called Rylie. The phone rang through the gym speakerless and small, just the tinny sound of it on the bench where she set it down, and then Rylie's voice, low, saying she was sorry, saying her mom was on the phone with the admissions office about the transfer credits, saying she would see them all eventually.

"That's not the same," Priya said, quietly, not to Rylie, to Beth.

"I know," Beth said.

They stayed past ten. The light through the high windows went from yellow to the diaphanous gray of late evening, and then Coach's timer shut the main banks off and left only the exit signs, red, at each end of the floor. In that half dark the five of them played a game of around the world, Rylie still on the phone on the bench, saying "missed it" whenever Marcus bricked, laughing at him from wherever she was. Natalie made it all the way around to the last corner, the same corner she had missed from in the semifinal, and she stood there a long time with the ball.

She shot it before she could decide anything about it. The ball hit the back rim, rolled around the ring twice, and dropped through.

"That counts," Rylie said, from the bench.

Natalie picked the ball up and held it against her hip, and looked at the door.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and the ghost of a hundred solder joints, and in the middle of it stood an upright piano that had come from Mrs. Okafor's church when the church got an electronic one with settings for cathedral echo. Laurie's parents called it hers now, which meant it was her problem. She had until Monday to mark a full analysis of the first movement of Mozart's A major sonata for the community college placement exam, and she had traded her brother Theo an hour of garage silence for the privilege of not hearing his band, which was called Sedimentary Crisis and had four members, three of whom could not play.

"It's not personal," Theo said, hauling his drum kit toward the driveway. "You're not being stigmatized. Lots of people sit alone in garages annotating Mozart on a Saturday."

"Name two."

He named two fictional characters and left the door propped open with a brick, which was the closest he came to kindness.

Laurie spread the score across the piano's music rack and onto a folding table she had carried out earlier, weighing the pages with socket wrenches from the shelf. She had a system, or the beginning of one. First she would bracket the exposition, the stretch at the opening where Mozart laid out his material: the poised first theme in A major, the excursion to the dominant where the second theme lived, then the double bar with its repeat signs like a raised eyebrow, asking, again? Then the development, where everything that had been calm got taken apart, key after key, until the music circled home. Then the recapitulation, where the first theme returned and the second theme, this time, stayed in A major instead of wandering off. That was the whole map. Her pencil was sharp and her margins were ruled.

She got through the exposition in forty minutes, mostly by listening. She played the opening six bars, stopped, marked the first theme with a bracket and a careful T1. The second theme took longer, because Mozart, being Mozart, blurred the moment of arrival with a run of sixteenth notes that sounded like the theme had been there all along, resting. She settled on a bar number, drew the bracket, and only then noticed the dust in the air, gold and slow in the light from the window, settling on the score like some alluvial deposit of the afternoon. She blew it off the page and kept going.

The development was easier than she had feared and worse than she had hoped. The opening theme fractured immediately, as if it had been dropped, and the pieces wandered through keys she could not name fast enough to label. She wrote modulating in one margin and felt the word was both accurate and a small defeat. Somewhere around the middle the music tightened, circling a dominant pedal like water reluctant to go down a drain, and then the first theme returned, whole and quiet, in A major, and she bracketed the recapitulation with a satisfaction she did not entirely trust.

The mistrust was justified. She worked through the recapitulation measure by measure, tracking the second theme's corrected key, and reached what should have been the end of her brackets. But the music kept going. Ten more bars. Twelve. A final cadence, emphatic, repeated, with a little descending figure that hammered the A again and again like it was making sure. Her markings had run out before Mozart had. She counted the bars twice, erased her closing bracket, recounted, and sat back on the piano bench with the socket wrench still holding down page four.

"Still going," Theo said from the driveway, where he had been eating a granola bar and watching her through the door with the expression of a nature documentarian. "Thought you said the recap was the end."

"It is the end. Except for the part after the end." She pulled her textbook out of her backpack and hunted the index, past cadence, past chromaticism, until she found the entry and read it with her finger under the line, once, twice. Then she picked the pencil back up.

"It's a coda," she said. "Optional. After the recapitulation. Reinforces the home key, brings the movement to the end." She drew the final bracket around those twelve bars, and the last one crossed a barline so firmly the page dented. Theo raised his granola bar in a small toast, and Laurie, for reasons she declined to examine, played the last three chords twice.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
Riley stood at the kitchen counter on a Saturday afternoon, holding a butter knife over a block of cheddar, and told his sister that if she gave him ten minutes he could explain to her exactly how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. Priya was eleven and did not demur, which surprised him. She sat down at the table with the air of someone expecting to be bored but willing to be paid in cheese.

The want was simple and slightly humiliating. His alumni interview for the Whitcombe Scholarship was on Monday, and on the application, in a fit of ambition he now regretted, he had written that he followed monetary policy closely and could explain it to a layperson. He had written this because at the time it had felt true, in the way things feel true at midnight. Now it was Saturday, and when he opened his mouth to begin, nothing came out.

He did have one piece of actual knowledge, acquired by accident. Last spring he'd been at the First National branch on Delmar, depositing a birthday check, when the television above the tellers said the Fed had raised rates again. The man ahead of Riley in line, holding a cable bill like a legal document, asked the teller which rate the Fed actually set, since his mortgage rate had gone up and he wanted to know whom to blame. "The federal funds rate," the teller said. "That's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She said it flat, the way she might have said the branch closed at five, and the man had nodded as though something had been settled, though Riley suspected nothing had.

He'd carried that sentence around for a year like a coin in a coat pocket, and now he took it out and put it on the kitchen table for Priya. "Okay. So. Banks lend each other money overnight." She was already chewing the first slice of cheddar. "Why?" "Because sometimes they're short on reserves at the end of the day. And the Fed doesn't set your mortgage rate. It sets this overnight rate, and everything else kind of... drifts off it." He heard himself say drifts and disliked it. It was the word you used when you didn't know the mechanism, and he was honest enough with himself, at least on Saturdays, to admit he didn't.

So he tried the chain out loud, piece by piece, standing and occasionally pointing at the refrigerator as though it were a chart. Higher overnight rate, banks pass the cost along, loans get more expensive everywhere, people and businesses borrow less, spending cools, and prices stop climbing so fast. Priya ate a second slice and said, "So the Fed makes everything more expensive so things stop being expensive." Riley opened his mouth to correct her and then closed it, because she had compressed his ten minutes of hedging into something he couldn't actually find a flaw in. "That's the ugly part, yeah."

Their mother came through in her gardening gloves, complained that the bed by the garage had soil like old cake, so friable it wouldn't hold water or a thought, and told Riley his interview shirt was ironed and hanging on his door. He spent Sunday practicing in his room, addressing the mirror, working on his elocution the way his grandfather had once worked on a wedding toast, pacing, gesturing, once bowing. What he practiced most was the ending, the part where he said, honestly, that he could describe the chain but couldn't prove every link, that economists themselves argued about how long it took and how much it hurt employment, and that he'd rather say that than pretend certainty he didn't have. It felt like the smart answer. It also might be the boring answer. He wouldn't know until Monday which it was.

Monday came, and the interview was in a coffee shop, not an office, which Riley found both relaxing and destabilizing. The interviewer was younger than expected, a woman with a laptop covered in stickers, and she said her name was Dana Okonkwo and that she'd worked at First National for six years before going back for her degree. Riley's stomach performed a small, private maneuver. He could not possibly confirm it. She asked the usual questions, and then she asked the one he'd been rehearsing toward, and he laid out the chain, overnight rate to bank rates to borrowing to spending to prices, and got to use his sentence, the teller's sentence, about banks charging each other for overnight loans of reserves, and it came out level and clear.

"Good," she said. "Now the part you can't explain."

He laughed, once, before he could stop himself. "The timing," he said. "How long it takes, and who pays while it works. I've read four answers and I believe about one and a half of them." Dana wrote something down, and Riley, who wanted very badly to see it, looked at the sticker nearest her thumb instead, a small drawn bird wearing glasses.

"I'm going to be honest with you," she said, closing the laptop halfway. "I only skim the finance applications. But yours was the one that quoted a teller."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: At 7 percent annual growth compounded yearly, $1,000 grows to almost $15,000 in forty years, so money saved at eighteen can multiply many times by retirement.
story:
The check lay flat on Tyler's palm, one hundred and eighty-four dollars, his first real wages from Delgado's nursery where he had spent the summer hauling mulch and watering rows of saplings. He had a plan already: a used subwoofer for the Corolla, the one Marcus found online for one sixty. The plan had survived all the way to his grandfather's house, where Tyler had come that Saturday to help clear the garage before winter.

His grandfather wanted the garage cleared, truly wanted it, though Tyler suspected the wanting had less to do with the garage than with having somebody in it. Since Tyler's uncle Ray had stopped visiting, the old man had begun assigning tasks, small ones, urgently, as if a raked lawn or a sorted toolbox could summon a family back into the yard.

The garage smelled of oil and cut pine. Tyler opened a metal cabinet and found a shoebox of papers, decades thick. Receipts, warranty cards, a ledger in his grandfather's careful hand. Beside one entry from 1983, in the margin, his grandfather had written a pithy note to himself: "Should have planted the north field. Didn't. Regret it." Tyler carried the box to the folding table where the old man was sorting bolts into jars.

"What's this ledger?"

"Expenses. Farm stuff." His grandfather didn't look up. "That was the year I almost put money into seedlings for the north field. Wasn't sure I'd stay on the land. Waited. Then the price of water changed and it never made sense again."

Tyler set the box down. He had been doing arithmetic in his head since Tuesday, ever since Marcus's cousin, who worked at a bank, had told him something at the barbecue. He took the stub of pencil from the table and the back of an envelope.

"I get paid again in two weeks," he said. "Marcus's cousin said if I put in a thousand dollars and it grows at seven percent a year, compounded, in forty years it's almost fifteen thousand. Like, money I save now at eighteen would be worth all that when I'm fifty-eight."

His grandfather set down a jar and took the envelope. He looked at the numbers Tyler had scrawled, the 1,000, the 7 percent, the 40, the almost-15,000, as though reading a weather map. "That right?"

"That's what he said. I ran it twice."

The old man was quiet for a while. Through the open garage door Tyler could hear a cardinal in the elm, and somewhere down the block a leaf blower starting and stopping.

"I can't prognosticate worth a damn," his grandfather said finally. "Nobody at that barbecue could tell you what the world looks like in forty years. Could be seven percent, could be nothing, could be worse. But that note in the ledger, that's the other side of it. I waited because I couldn't be sure, and being unable to be sure cost me the field." He pushed the envelope back across the table. "Both of those are true at once. I don't know which one you should hold onto."

Tyler looked at the subwoofer money in his checking account and tried to picture himself at fifty-eight. The picture wouldn't come. He could picture the Corolla rattling with bass, Marcus grinning, the whole senior year lit up by it. He could picture the thousand sitting somewhere invisible, patient, turning into something he couldn't see and might not recognize when it arrived.

"So what did you do?" he asked. "After you didn't plant."
