He could have worked from the image on his laptop, but his grandmother had said come over, the light is better in the morning, and she had made him eggs before leaving him alone with it.

He began the way the assignment demanded, with a pencil and cheap sketchbook, copying the composition in outline. Two women in chairs, holding hands, seated on a bench under a churned grey sky. The one on the left wore a white European dress, lace at the collar, wedding-style, formal almost to the point of ceremony. The one on the right wore the Tehuana dress, bright colour, and John had to decide what to call that difference in his notes. Costuming as identity, he wrote, and then crossed it out because it sounded like something borrowed. He wrote instead, she painted two of herself and made them opposites, then crossed that out too, because he wasn't sure it was true.

The trouble was the essay itself, which was due Monday and had to argue something. His grandmother drifted in and out with laundry, unapologetic about the interruptions. "You've been staring," she said at one point. "Staring is not looking." She was obstreperous in the mild way of a person who believes her house entitles her to commentary, and John had learned not to argue, only to keep sketching.

The sketch was what changed things. Copying the figures, he had to decide where every line went, and when he reached the chests he stopped. Both women's hearts were exposed, painted outside the body, one whole and flushed, the other cut and bleeding. That was strange enough. But from the torn heart on the left, a single red thread ran down, and John traced it with his pencil, along the arm, through the hand of one Frida to the hand of the other, back up to the intact heart, one blood vessel winding between both hearts, connecting them. He sat back. He had looked at the image for two days and had not seen the line until his own hand had to draw it.

"Did you know this was here?" he asked when his grandmother came through with towels.

She came to the poster and followed his pencil point. "Your grandfather pointed it out to me once," she said. "I said it was morbid. He said it was honest." She folded a towel over her arm. "He was usually right about paintings and wrong about other things."

John worked through the afternoon. Formal analysis wanted him to stay with what he could see: the exposed hearts, the connecting vessel, the scissors in the left Frida's lap, the small portrait the right Frida held, the stormy sky pressing down on both figures equally. Colour supported it, the cold whites and blues on one side, the warm earth tones on the other, and yet the red line crossed the whole divide. He drafted a thesis that the painting's symbols of separation were undercut by its composition, which physically joined the two figures. It was the first idea in the essay that felt like his own.

But something nagged at him. His grandmother's remark sat in his mind while he wrote, and he kept circling back to his own crossed-out notes. Two ways of seeing the painting competed in him: the formal one, where the line was simply a compositional fact linking colour fields, and another, more personal one, where the line insisted that a divided self stays connected by something it cannot sever. He could not fully hold both positions at once, and he was honest enough with himself to write that in the margin, a note to resolve later. The margin note was still there when he finished.

His grandmother read the draft in the kitchen while he washed the dishes he had promised to wash. He watched her over his shoulder, her finger moving down the page, pausing where he had written about the single vessel winding through their hands and hearts. He wanted her to absolve him of the uncertainty he had left in the final paragraph, to say it was fine not to conclude, but she didn't. She set the pages on the table, and he noticed she had set them beside his grandfather's old reading glasses, still kept there, still used for nothing.

"Well," she said. "You saw it. Most people never see the thread."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
Lauren had the instructor's confirmation email open on her phone as she stood at the end of the driveway, one shoe on the curb, waiting for a blue automatic Corsa that hadn't appeared yet. Behind her sat her father's manual Golf, faded green, third gear still sticky from the year he'd learned to tow a trailer. The school's booking form had offered automatic lessons at the same price, and she'd ticked automatic without thinking, the way she ticked most boxes, because automatic seemed to subsume everything a beginner needed: steering, mirrors, judgment, all of it minus one pedal and a gearstick. She was eighteen in six weeks and she had a plan she hadn't yet said aloud, a plan involving her grandmother's cottage forty minutes away down lanes the buses didn't serve.

The blue car arrived on time. The instructor, a woman named Pat with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair, got out and walked around to the passenger side. "Lauren? We'll do the cockpit drill, then a few laps of the estate. Quiet this time of morning." She said it kindly, in the tone of someone who had said it four thousand times.

Lauren got in, adjusted the seat, and then didn't touch the seatbelt. "Pat. Can I ask something before we start? If I pass my test in this car, in an automatic, what can I drive after?"

"Automatics," Pat said. "Only automatics. You'd have to pass a manual test to drive a manual car."

Lauren looked through the windscreen at the Golf, at the gearstick she'd watched her father's hand find without looking, at the whole errand of her grandmother's shopping and hospital appointments and the Sunday roast tins that somehow got subsumed under the single word helping. She had assumed a licence was a licence, one genus covering every car on the road. It wasn't. It forked, like the degrees her friends were choosing, and the fork you picked quietly in a booking form turned out to matter.

"I learned in a manual," Pat went on, not lecturing, just filling the silence the way instructors do. "Hated it for three lessons. Then it stopped being a thing I thought about." She checked her mirror, unhurried. "We can swap your bookings, if that's what you're thinking. Same price, same hours. But the first few manual lessons are harder. I won't pretend otherwise. You'll stall it."

From the kitchen window, Pat watched the girl stand very still with her hand on the roof of the car. She had seen this before, though not often, and never this early, before a single lesson. Most learners wanted the easy version and never asked what the easy version left out. The father came out of the house then, still holding his coffee mug, and stood at his own front door like a man uncertain whether he'd been summoned. Pat lowered her window an inch. "She's got a question, Mr. Ahmadi. It's a good one."

Lauren's father came down the driveway slowly, setting the mug on the low wall by the gate. "What question?"

"If I pass in an automatic, I can't drive your car," Lauren said. "Not legally. I'd have to do another test, in a manual, to drive a manual." She heard herself say it and realised she was testing the sentence as much as telling him, checking whether it still sounded absurd in the open air. It didn't. It sounded like something she should have found out in March.

Her father looked at the Golf as if it had said something. "Your uncle drove that car for eight years," he said, which wasn't an answer, and then, quieter, "Your gran asks after you. She thinks you'll come in that car." He said it plainly, without weight, but she understood he'd been thinking about the lanes too, the hospital in Truro, the fact that his own knees were starting to object to the trip. Perhaps he'd even been counting on her, though he'd never have used that word. Grandparents were supposed to be the munificent ones, pressing twenties into card pockets, and her grandmother was, but lately the giving ran in the other direction and nobody had announced the change; it had simply happened, like a season turning.

"I'll swap to manual," Lauren said to Pat. "All the hours. If I stall it, I stall it."

Pat nodded and opened the boot for the L plates, and Lauren, taking one, turned it over in her hands, the white square with its red L, and walked up the driveway to the green car where her father was already fishing the keys out of his jacket pocket. "Not today," Pat called after her, gently. "Bookings first." Lauren stopped, laughed once at herself, and came back, and her father lowered himself into the Golf, started it, and held the clutch down in neutral while he waited, engine running, for his daughter to finish sorting out the paperwork.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
Gabrielle counted the bills twice in the aisle by the registers, because counting money in public felt like a confession, and she had exactly eleven dollars and thirty cents. The sneakers on her feet had a hole along the seam that let in water, and the pair she wanted, marked down on the end cap, cost ten ninety-nine. She had done the arithmetic walking here, done it again on the bus, and the margin was thin enough to feel like a dare.

The shoes were on a lower shelf, boxed and heavy, and she carried them to the register like something perishable. Ahead of her a man was buying batteries and a lottery ticket, and the cashier, a woman named Dolores according to the tag, read out his total in a flat, tireless voice. The man's register had a little screen facing the customer, and Gabrielle watched the numbers on it the way she watched chemistry experiments, waiting for the change she could predict.

"Ten ninety-nine," she said when her turn came, laying the box on the belt, "right?" Dolores scanned it and the screen said eleven dollars and seventy-something, and Gabrielle's stomach dropped a small, precise distance. "That's not the price," she said. "The sticker says ten ninety-nine."

"Sticker's before tax," Dolores said. "Sales tax gets added at the register."

Gabrielle stood there with her eleven dollars and thirty cents and understood, in one cold flash, that the number on the shelf had never been the number at the register, that there was a whole category of price that only existed at the last second, after you had already decided. She asked how much the total was with the tax and Dolores told her, and it was more than she had by about forty cents. Forty cents. She looked at the coins in her palm as if they had betrayed her personally.

"Can you put something back?" Dolores asked, not unkindly, and Gabrielle said she couldn't, because the something was the entire purchase. Behind her a boy from school, Marcus, was waiting with a basket, and she felt the particular heat of being watched while failing at arithmetic in public. She took out her phone, opened the calculator, and worked backward from what she had: if she had eleven thirty, what shelf price could she afford once the tax was layered on? The answer came out around ten dollars even, which meant a different, plainer pair of shoes on a different shelf.

She found them, canvas instead of the waterproof ones, and stood a moment in the aisle holding both boxes. It seemed like a strange way to run a country, she thought, a system where every price was a partial truth; other places, she'd heard somewhere, put the real number right on the tag. But that was a rumor, and she had no way to check it here, only the register, which had already told her the truth once. She carried the canvas pair back and let the other box go, and the register's screen said eleven dollars and twenty-one cents, which fit under her money with nine cents of daylight.

"Do you want the receipt?" Dolores asked, and Gabrielle said yes, because she wanted to see the anatomy of it, the line where the shoes ended and the tax began. The receipt showed the subtotal, ten dollars even, then a line for sales tax, then the total, and she folded it into her pocket like evidence.

On the bus home she sat near Marcus, who had been behind her the whole time. "That was slick," he said, meaning the calculator move. "Most people just get short at the register."

"I got short," she said. "I just got short quietly."

He laughed and told her he'd started work at a grocery store in March, and that his first paycheque had shocked him, because he'd done the math on his hours and his wage and arrived at a number that the cheque did not agree with. "They take off income tax before you even see it," he said. "There's a whole deduction section. And then there's another deduction for something called CPP, which nobody explains to you when you're sixteen."

Gabrielle turned that over. So the register took from the top, and the paycheque took from the top, and both of them let you believe in the bigger number first. She wondered whether the deductions were a kind of theft or a kind of promise, whether the money would come back to him someday in some form, and she said so, and Marcus shrugged and said his mother filed a tax return every spring and sometimes got money back, which suggested the system was more like a settling of accounts than a straightforward taking. Neither of them knew, really, and neither pretended to, which felt like its own kind of accomplishment.

Later, in her room, she set the canvas shoes beside the receipt and examined the hole in the old pair, its edges worn to something smooth and almost igneous, like rock that had cooled after heat. Her father came past her door and asked how the shopping had gone, and she said, "Did you know the shelf price isn't the real price?" and he said, "Welcome to adulthood," in the tone of a man who had stopped expecting the world to explain itself.

She put the new shoes on. They were not the waterproof ones, and it was supposed to rain Thursday, and she had nine cents in her pocket, and a paycheque of her own suddenly seemed less like a distant adult thing and more like a door she wanted to walk through, deductions and all. She folded the receipt smaller and put it in the box with the old shoes, and laced up, and stood.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The manager slid a clipboard across the table before Andrew had even sat down, and on it was a form he had never seen before, dense with small boxes, the kind of document that seemed designed to make you feel guilty before you had done anything. "You can't start your shift until this is done," she said. "It's the law. Every new employee has to complete it, no later than their first day of paid work." Andrew turned the clipboard toward the window light of the restaurant, past the mock-mediterranean murals and the igneous black countertop the owner had installed to look expensive, and read the top of the page. Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification. Section 1, Employee Information and Attestation. Below that, a smaller line: to be completed by the employee no later than the first day of employment.

"I did the W-4 online," he said. "My mom helped me. Nobody said anything about this one."

"Everyone forgets this one." The manager, whose nametag read DENISE, was already walking a tray of bread to table six. "Fill out Section 1, give me your ID and your social security card, and you're fine. If you didn't bring them, you're not fine."

He had not brought them. He had brought a water bottle and his phone and a folded paper with his availability written on it, because the interview had felt like the hard part and he had assumed the rest was paperwork in the loose, ceremonial sense. He looked at the form again. His date of birth, his address, a citizenship checkbox he could have handled in third grade. Then the attestation, a paragraph in tiny type that he was supposed to certify under penalty of perjury. It asked about his permission to work, which seemed absurd, since he had been staring at the permission to work for two weeks, in the form of a laminated schedule taped to the kitchen door with his name on it.

He found Denise by the drink station. "What happens if I fill this out at home tonight and bring it tomorrow?"

"Then tomorrow's your first day of paid work, and you're on time. Today you're just a person eating free bread." She said it without cruelty, refilling a water pitcher while she talked. "But if you'd shown up for an actual shift without it, we'd have a problem."

He wanted to argue the logic of a law that counted orientation as not-work but required the form for work that had not started. He had spent the whole drive here composing an argument of that kind for his father, who believed that any rule a seventeen-year-old could articulate an objection to was a rule a seventeen-year-old could ignore. His mother held the opposite position with equal force: rules were load-bearing walls, and you did not test them by leaning. For years he had treated their positions as a choice between them, a door with two handles, and lately he had begun to suspect the door might have hinges of its own. The I-9 was not an injustice. It was fifteen minutes and a folder at home. But it was also, his father would point out, the state's way of making a dishwasher prove himself, a small ceremony of subjugation dressed as procedure. His mother would say that a country that could not verify who worked in it could not protect the people who did. Standing at the drink station with a form he could not sign, Andrew found he agreed with both of them, and that agreeing with both of them was not the same as agreeing with nobody.

"I can be back by four," he said. "My house is ten minutes."

"Kitchen tour's at three thirty."

"Then I'll miss the kitchen tour and see the kitchen when I'm in it." He heard his own voice come out clipped, harder than he meant, and Denise looked at him for a moment, sizing up whether he was going to be a problem employee or just a person having one bad half hour.

"That's actually how my last hire did it," she said. "He's at college now. Bring the documents, sign it in front of me, and you start tomorrow at five. That's the whole thing."

He drove home with the clipboard still in his hand, because Denise had said she had copies, and he had said nothing and kept it, and she had said nothing and let him. At the kitchen table he found the folder his mother kept on top of the fridge, his birth certificate, his social security card in its paper sleeve, soft at the corners from years of being handed across counters. His father came through the back door with groceries and saw the form open on the table.

"What's that one?"

"Employment verification. I have to finish it by my first day of work, which is tomorrow at five."

His father set down the bag of oranges. "Section 1's the employee part," he said, tapping the page. "I've filled out fifty of these. Check the box, sign, date it."

Andrew looked up at him. "You've seen this form?"

"Every job since I was nineteen, kid." His father pulled out a chair and sat down across from him, and there was something almost shy in it, a man offering the one inheritance he was sure of. "You want, I'll look it over when you're done."

Andrew took out a pen, printed his full name in the first blank, and began.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
Parker had been filing escrow paperwork at Hartwell Realty for six weeks, and by the second week he had stopped reading the documents and started studying them. He was eighteen, and in September he was supposed to move into a two-bedroom apartment above the laundromat on Corbett Street with Dee, who was already counting weeks at her hostess job. The apartment was eight hundred fifty a month, which they would split, but the listing had said "first month, last month, and deposit," and Parker had eleven hundred dollars in a checking account that his debit card kept trying to be honest about. He had done the math on the bus that morning, then done it again as though the numbers might pity him.

At the front desk he sorted the morning's files, and through the glass wall of the conference room he watched Ms. Ruiz walk a young couple through a purchase. He could hear most of it. "The down payment is the part you bring to the table," Ruiz said, tapping the folder. "Twenty percent of the price is ideal. The bank lends the rest, and that loan is the mortgage, and you pay it monthly, with interest, for thirty years if you want." The woman asked what happened if they couldn't pay, and Ruiz didn't soften it. "The bank takes the house. That's the risk. That's the whole arrangement." Parker wrote twenty percent on a sticky note, then the price of a modest house in this town, then the down payment that came out to more than four years of his salary, and folded the note into his pocket like it was evidence of something.

He caught Ruiz at the copier. "Why is it called a mortgage?" he asked. "It's a weird word." She looked at him the way she looked at buyers who asked about schools, deciding whether the question was serious. "I heard a client say once that it means something dark," she said. "I never checked. Ask someone who reads." Then she handed him the listing sheet for the Corbett Street apartment and said, "Your landlord called. He wants the deposit money by the fifteenth or he re-lists."

That night at his grandmother's kitchen table, he ate the pork chops she made without being asked and didn't touch the okra, and he said, "Do you know why a home loan is called a mortgage? It sounds like something died." His grandmother kept cutting. "Old French," she said. "Dead pledge." He waited. She ate a piece of okra he'd pushed to the rim of his plate. "That's what they told your grandfather at the bank in 1979. The pledge dies when the debt is paid." He asked, "And if it isn't paid?" She looked up then. "Or when the property is forfeited." She went back to her plate, and Parker sat with the phrase, dead pledge, turning it over while the refrigerator hummed. Two doors out of the arrangement, and one of them meant losing the house.

On Thursday, Dee's letter came, because Dee wrote letters when the news was bad, having decided that texts made bad news look casual. Parker, it began. They cut my hours to three shifts a week. I have six hundred saved and I can cover maybe a third of the move-in money and my half of rent after that is not guaranteed. My mother says I should stay home and commute and honestly she is right and I hate that she is right. I'm sorry. We can talk Friday. Parker read it twice on the porch steps, then a third time holding it against the railing like a form he had to sign.

He dichotomized the situation out of habit, the way he'd learned to at the office where Ruiz sorted everyone into renters and owners as though the two never traded places: either the apartment happened or it didn't, either Dee was in or she was out. But the categories kept leaking into each other. His grandmother had paid off her dead pledge nineteen years ago; he'd been at the small party, a mortgage-burning in the backyard, though he hadn't known the word then. It struck him now as a kind of synchronicity, that he'd been filing mortgage documents the very week the Corbett Street deadline arrived, and the coincidence felt less like fate than like a prompt.

Friday he did the arithmetic differently. First month, last month, and deposit came to twenty-five hundred and fifty. His eleven hundred plus Dee's six hundred left a gap, and rent after that was a monthly problem the deposit didn't touch. He went back to Ruiz before his shift and asked whether the landlord would take the deposit as a smaller amount held against the last month, since that was technically what a deposit was, money held, not money spent. Ruiz almost smiled. "That's a trenchant point for a file clerk," she said. "He'll say no. But if you ask him to apply Dee's six hundred to the last month up front, and you come in Saturdays to help me with the closing packets at twelve an hour, you cover the gap in five weeks." She slid a contract across the desk. "It's not a loan. It's work."

He called Dee from the parking lot and read her the terms, and she was quiet long enough that he could hear the hostess stand in the background, the clink of glasses. "Saturdays too?" she said. "You're already working weekdays." He said he'd rather be tired in a place that was his, even a rented his, than rested at his mother's. She said, "Then Saturday we go sign," and he could hear her deciding to be in.

On the fifteenth, Parker handed over a cashier's check for the deposit and first month, and the landlord wrote RECEIVED on a carbon copy and told him the pledge ended when they moved out clean or when they forfeited, and Parker thought, everything is dead pledges, and didn't say it. He texted his grandmother a photo of the keys on the laundromat stairs. She wrote back a single line: Your grandfather's took thirty years to die. He put the phone in his pocket and unlocked the door to the smell of dryer sheets and old carpet, and Dee was already carrying a box up the stairs.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Informed consent in medicine means a patient agrees to treatment after being told its risks, benefits and alternatives in words they can understand.
story:
Nicolas had worked the front desk at Ridgeline Fitness for six weeks, long enough to recite the membership agreement in his sleep, though he had stopped reciting it. New members glazed over somewhere around section four, liability, and he learned to say instead, "Basically, you agree not to sue us if you drop a plate on your foot, and we agree to let you in the door." That was a summary, not the terms, and he knew the difference mattered, because the terms were what people signed and the summary was what they remembered, and the gap between the two was where things went wrong.

The trouble started on a Tuesday evening, when the gym was torpid with August heat and the only sounds were a treadmill's belt and the desk radio turned low. His phone lit up against the counter: his sister Camille, seventeen, calling from the walk-in clinic across town. He turned the radio down.

"Nick, they gave me this form for my wrist, it's like three pages, and I'm supposed to sign it, and there's a word in here I don't know and the nurse is busy." Her voice dropped, the way it did when she was trying not to sound young. "It says something about a risk. I don't want to sign something I don't understand."

He looked down the empty lobby. In front of him sat a stack of day-pass waivers, each one a small contract: assumptions of risk, releases, initials required in four places. People signed them without reading, every day, and he had let himself become comfortable with that. It had started to ferment in him, that quiet discomfort, back when a regular named Mr. Okafor had actually read every line, asked what "indemnify" meant, and made Nicolas look it up on the spot because Nicolas hadn't known either. Mr. Okafor had smiled and said, "First honest answer I've gotten at a gym desk," and signed. That had stayed with Nicolas more than any compliment about his smile or his customer service.

"Read me the part you're stuck on," he said.

She read it. It was dense, clause within clause, and in the middle of it a sentence about a risk of the treatment, listed alongside a sentence about benefits, and somewhere below, in smaller print, mention of other options. "I think," Nicolas said slowly, "I think that's the whole point of the form. It's not just permission. It's supposed to be them telling you the risks, and the benefits, and what else you could do instead, in a way you can actually understand. That's what makes it real consent instead of just a signature." He wasn't sure he had the right to sound this certain. He was reasoning from the gym, where a signature meant nothing unless the person had some idea what they were signing.

"So I should ask her to explain the risk?" Camille said. "Even the word I don't know?"

"Especially the word you don't know. If she can't put it in words you understand, then you don't understand it, and the form isn't doing its job." He heard her exhale, then the muffled sound of her walking, then a nurse's voice, warm and unhurried, saying, "Of course, honey, let's go through it." Nicolas held the phone against his chest without hanging up, in case she came back.

While he waited, a man in a gray shirt came to the desk wanting a day pass, and Nicolas did something he had never done. He slid the waiver across and said, "Before you sign, I'll walk you through the terms. This part limits what you can claim if you get hurt, this part is about the equipment, and you can ask me anything and I'll answer or find out." The man blinked, then read the whole thing, asked two questions, initialed every box, and said, "You know, my grandfather used to say a signature is a promise, and you don't promise what you haven't heard." Nicolas wrote nothing down, but he kept the sentence anyway.

Camille came back on the line ten minutes later. "She explained it. The risk word meant the treatment could bruise the tendon, and the benefit is faster healing, and the alternative was just a splint and waiting. She said it in regular words. Then I signed." There was something changed in her voice, a steadiness. "It felt different from signing the gym thing you always rush me through."

He laughed, and admitted that he was part of that problem, and told her he'd started reading the waivers out loud at the desk. He didn't tell her about Mr. Okafor, or about the way the evening had rearranged something in him, the sense that he had been standing at a border between two worlds, the world of fine print and the world of people, and had decided they were not supposed to be separate countries with him as a bored customs officer. He was not sure, entirely, whether every form could live up to the idea. He knew the clinic form had, tonight, for one seventeen-year-old, and that a day-pass waiver had, for one man in a gray shirt, and he suspected that was how things actually changed: not by decree, but one explanation at a time, given before the signature instead of after the injury.

At closing he straightened the waiver stack, and on the top copy, in the margin, someone had doodled a small cartoon of a handshake. He left it there for the morning shift to find.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
story:
The mitochondria exhibit glowed like something newly discovered, though the plaque claimed it had been installed for nine years, and Maxime had walked past it at least that many times on school trips he half remembered. Today he was here alone, with a worksheet his biology teacher had handed out like a dare, and a pencil he kept chewing. At the top of the sheet, in his own handwriting, was the task: trace one glucose molecule to its ATP, step by step, through the stations in order.

He started badly. At the glycolysis station, a wall of animated molecules split and recombined on a loop, and he copied down the net gain of two ATP, feeling briefly triumphant, as though he had personally catalyzed the reaction rather than watched it happen on a screen. He moved on to pyruvate oxidation, wrote "2 acetyl-CoA," underlined it, and gave it no further thought. That was the mistake, though he did not know it yet. He was still in the mood of a student following a recipe, not a chemist counting what actually goes into a pot.

His phone buzzed against his thigh. It was Ana, who was supposed to have come with him before she had to cover her brother's shift at the pharmacy.

"Did you get to the summer research thing," she had texted. "I applied. Deadline is 5 today. You could still do it from the museum if you wanted."

He had told her, last month, that the program sounded grandiose, that a summer cataloguing bacteria morphology in a basement lab was not his idea of a vacation. She had gone quiet at that, and he had let it go quiet, because arguing would have meant admitting he was afraid of the application essay more than of the basement. Now he typed, "Still working on the worksheet," and put the phone face down on the bench, which was its own kind of answer, and not one he was proud of.

At the citric acid cycle station, the museum had built a rotating carousel of molecule models, turning slowly like a lazy Susan of carbon skeletons. He counted the ATP the cycle produced per turn, multiplied by nothing in particular, added it to his total, and moved through the electron transport chain, where a light show of protons tumbling through a membrane made ATP synthesis look almost extravagant. Then he summed everything and sat back.

The number was wrong. He checked it against the answer posted at the exit, printed upside down like a crossword key, and his tally fell short by a suspicious margin. He went back through his notes twice. Glycolysis, fine. Transport chain, fine. The gap sat squarely in the middle, in the carousel he had treated as a single event.

He stood at the cycle station a long time, watching it turn. Then he looked back at his own note, "2 acetyl-CoA," and felt the small vertigo of a thing rearranging itself in his head. He said it out loud, quietly, to the carousel: "The cycle turns twice for each glucose. One glucose makes two acetyl-CoA, and each one goes into the cycle separately." Everything after glycolysis was happening twice, and he had written it all down once. He crossed out his total and rebuilt it, and the new number matched, and he grinned at the molecule models like they had let him in on a conspiracy.

Ana would have caught it in five minutes. She thought in doubles and mirrors, in the symmetry of things, and he thought in straight lines, and somewhere between the two of them was probably the student who belonged in that basement lab. His phone was still face down. He picked it up and saw she had sent one more message: "It's fine if you don't apply. But don't decide because you're scared. Decide because you don't want it."

He read it three times. It was the kind of thing she would have said in person, looking at him sideways, daring him to be honest with himself, and the fact that it came as text on a screen made it both easier and harder to answer. He thought about the essay question, which asked for a moment of genuine confusion and how he had worked through it, and he thought, with some embarrassment, that he was standing inside one.

The museum was closing in forty minutes. Maxime sat back down on the bench, opened the application page, and began to type, while the carousel behind him kept turning, and turning again.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
The kitchen scale at Grandma's house weighed in grams and had a sticky zero button, and by seven o'clock on Sunday evening it was the only scale Emma had. Her science fair notebook lay open beside it, and the baggie of vinegar and baking soda, sealed with two pieces of tape, sat on the counter like a small white fish. The fair started at eight tomorrow morning. She had a ride at seven, which meant she had until six tomorrow to know, actually know, what she was going to say when the judges stopped at her table.

The weighing part she had done already, three times. Before the reaction, the sealed bag had weighed 84.2 grams. After she had squeezed the inner pouch through the plastic and watched the bag fill with gas, it still weighed 84.2 grams. She had written those numbers down and then stared at them, because some part of her had expected the gas to weigh nothing, to escape the arithmetic somehow, and it hadn't. Nothing had left. She kept touching the bag as if it might tell her something through the plastic.

What she couldn't do yet was the second half, the part on the worksheet Mr. Ostrowski had handed out Friday with the words Moles of Product from Mass of Reactant underlined twice. The worksheet said: given a mass of a reactant, divide by its molar mass to get moles, then use the balanced equation to find the moles of product. She understood the words individually. Together they slid away from her whenever she tried to hold them.

Her grandmother came in from the garden with tomatoes in her shirt hem and set them in the sink. She was a reticent woman who asked about school only once per visit, which made the asking feel like an event. "How's the project," she said now, second visit, which meant she had been paying attention.

"I can prove nothing disappears," Emma said. "But I can't turn grams into moles, and the judges will ask, and I'll stand there like a muffin."

Her grandmother dried her hands and sat down across from the notebook. She didn't touch it. She had left school at fifteen, Emma knew, to work, and she never pretended otherwise, but she also never left a room when someone was learning something.

Emma started over out loud, because out loud was the only way it would stick. "Baking soda. Sodium bicarbonate. One formula unit is, let me get this, 84.01 grams per mole." She turned the paper around so her grandmother could see the number. "And I used 5.00 grams of it. So the moles of baking soda is 5.00 divided by 84.01." She worked it. "0.0595 moles. That's how many moles of reactant I started with. Okay. Okay, that's something."

The balanced equation was next, and it told her that one mole of baking soda gave one mole of carbon dioxide, the gas in the bag. So the same 0.0595 moles of gas had been produced, hiding inside the sealed plastic the whole time, mass unchanged. She felt something click together, the two halves of her project meeting: the scale said the mass never changed, and the arithmetic said where every bit of that mass had gone. Each half seemed to subsume the other, the weighing and the calculation, until she couldn't tell which one was really the proof.

"Say the rule again," her grandmother said. "The one you're calling it."

"The law of conservation of mass," Emma said. "Total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants, in a closed system." She tapped the bag. "Closed system. That's why the tape matters. That's why the gas couldn't sneak off."

Her grandmother turned a tomato over in her hand, considering it. "Your grandfather kept a ledger," she said. "Feed store. Every sack in, every sack out, and if the numbers didn't match, somebody was stealing or somebody was wrong." She set the tomato down. "Never once thought of it as chemistry."

It was almost nine. Emma began building her poster text in her head, and she noticed a problem she didn't like: her numbers were only as honest as her weighing. The scale's zero button stuck. The bag had a drop of condensation she'd wiped off with a tissue, which meant she had taken a fraction of a gram out of her closed system and put it in the trash. Would the judges catch that? Should she say it out loud before they did? She wondered whether admitting the wobble made her project weaker or stronger, whether a clean story with a hidden flaw was better than a true story with a visible one. Her poster had promised exactness, and the world kept offering her something more like verisimilitude, an honest resemblance to exactness, close but never the thing itself.

She found a fresh baggie and rebuilt the demonstration from scratch, zeroing the scale twice, sealing the inner pouch with three pieces of tape this time, weighing before and after with her grandmother standing over her, watching the numbers. 91.7 grams, then 91.7 grams, the second reading rising steadily into place as the scale settled. Emma wrote it down and circled it.

"There," her grandmother said. "What does it mean, those two the same?"

"It means nothing got out and nothing got lost," Emma said. "Everything that was here is still here." She looked at the bag, plump with gas she couldn't see, and then at her calculation, 0.0595 moles of it, and slipped both the bag and the notebook into her backpack, zipping it shut.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
James had never lost a round at this tournament before lunch, and he told himself this mattered more than it did. Between rounds he sat in the empty chorus room with two actors from his school, Priya and Marcus, running the one-act he was directing for the spring festival, because the tournament was the only place all three of them had free hours at once. The room smelled of floor wax and old radiator. He had the script open on the piano bench and a pencil behind his ear, and he believed, sincerely, that he knew what he was doing.

The scene was the argument in the second act, the one where the brother tells the sister he is leaving. Marcus played the brother. James had blocked it the way that seemed honest to him: Marcus turned fully toward Priya, because people facing each other in a real fight do not arrange themselves for observers. He had even said this out loud in the last rehearsal, that truth on stage meant ignoring the audience entirely. Priya had nodded. Marcus had nodded. James had written "natural" in the margin and underlined it twice.

"From the top of the page," he said now, and tapped the pencil against the bench. Marcus took his mark by the door of the imaginary house, Priya sat on the edge of the imaginary bed, and the argument began. It was good. James could hear that it was good, the pace building, Marcus dropping his voice at the right moment instead of raising it. He watched with the satisfaction of a person who has planned something and watched the plan arrive, and he did not, for almost the whole run, look at anything but the two of them.

Then he did. He slid his chair sideways to the far wall, roughly where an audience would sit if there were one, and watched the scene again from there, and what he saw was the back of Marcus's head. Only the back. Marcus had his face turned to Priya through the entire argument, and from the wall the whole speech, the quiet voice, the dropped eyes, all of it landed on a thatch of dark hair. Priya's face carried fine. James sat very still and let the scene finish, and when it ended he said, "Hold on," and stood up, and did not say what was wrong because he was not yet sure how to say it.

"Your face," he said finally. Marcus touched his cheek, baffled. "From out there, I only get the back of your head. The whole leaving speech, I'm watching hair." He walked to Marcus's mark and turned to face Priya, then angled himself a few degrees toward the far wall, and the difference was immediate, his body still clearly addressed to her but opened enough that an audience would catch his mouth, his eyes, the sound of him. He tried it the other way again, facing her flat, and lost himself again behind his own skull.

Priya laughed, which he pretended not to mind. "It's called cheating out," she said. "You turn partly toward the audience even when you're talking to another character. My mom did community theater." James nodded as though he had known this and merely forgotten, which was the version of the afternoon he would later tell people, and wrote it in the margin over the underlined word "natural," which he then, after a small hesitation, crossed out. The pencil wavered. He wrote "cheat out, slightly" and felt both that he had been foolish and that his original instinct had not been entirely foolish, only half-right in the wrong direction.

They ran it again with the new angle, and the scene changed character in a way he had to think about. Marcus was a degree less intimate with Priya and a degree more available to the empty room, and the argument read differently, wider, less like eavesdropping and more like witnessing. James tried to interpolate between the two versions in his mind, imagining a blocking that kept the ferocity of the full turn and the visibility of the cheat, and found that the two pulled against each other, that every gain in honesty cost him some reach. He wondered, standing there with the pencil going soft in his grip, whether that tension was a problem to be solved or simply the condition of the whole art, whether every choice in this room would mean choosing who got to see.

A kid from another school put his head in the door looking for the tab room, apologized, and left. The loudspeaker crackled something about round four postings in the cafeteria. Marcus checked his phone and said he had to go pairings in ten minutes, and Priya said she had extemp prep, and James said he would stay and mark the floor with tape. He had a roll of blue tape in his bag because he had read, in one of the directing books he'd bought and only half finished, that serious directors tape their floors.

When they were gone he tore off strips and laid them where the marks were, Marcus's by the door angled a few degrees off the line to Priya's bed, and then he sat against the wall in the audience position and ran the scene in his head both ways. He thought about his debate rounds that morning, the way he had argued a side he did not believe with total conviction and won, and about the teleology of that, how the whole activity bent every statement toward its end, the ballot, the win. Directing felt different, or he wanted it to; the scene did not exist to defeat anyone. But watching Marcus cheat out toward nobody, toward a wall with blue tape and one boy sitting on it, he felt the incipient shape of an audience already implied in every position he set, a purpose built into the geometry before a single ticket was sold. He could not decide if that was a corruption or just a fact.

He stayed until the loudspeaker called his own name for round five. Then he folded the script, pocketed the tape roll, and left the blue marks on the floor for the janitor to puzzle over. At the door he turned back once, looked at the angle of the tape by the imaginary door, and moved it two inches toward the wall with the toe of his shoe.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
The retake notice arrived on a Tuesday, folded into Eva's locker like a threat. Sixty-one percent. She had one week to learn transcription and translation properly, or the biology mark would follow her into her college applications the way a smell follows a coat.

Her uncle's farm was forty minutes away by the school's activity bus, and her cousin Daisy, twelve, lived there with a workbook full of questions Daisy claimed were pointless. Eva's mother had suggested the visit before the retake notice existed, and now Eva packed her biology text along with the sleeping bag, thinking she could read in the evenings. She read the same paragraph four times on the bus and could not have repeated it after the fourth.

The paragraph was the problem. It described DNA being copied into RNA and RNA being turned into protein, and it used eleven terms per sentence, each one leaning on the others like drunks at a bus stop. She understood, in a vague way, that there was a cell and that something happened inside it. Beyond that, nothing. On Wednesday she sat on the farmhouse porch with the book open and her highlighter dying, and Daisy came out eating toast.

"You look like the toast," Daisy said, sitting down on the step.

"Thanks."

"What's that?"

"A book that hates me."

Daisy leaned over. There was a diagram, all curling lines and arrows, and Eva realized she could not even say which part was which. She snapped the book shut, which augured nothing good for the evening.

Thursday morning they were in the milking parlour waiting for Daisy's father, and Daisy was drawing on the concrete floor with a piece of chalk she kept in her jacket for reasons she did not explain. Eva, without planning to, asked whether Daisy knew why the cows were brown.

"Genes," Daisy said promptly. "It's in their, the thing. The DNA."

"Where is the DNA?"

Daisy pointed at a cow, generally. Eva looked at the cow, which stood chewing, and thought about her own cells, and thought about the fact that the instructions were all shut away in there, in the middle, in some protected inner room, and that the cow was brown anyway, out here, in its hair and its skin and its milk. The instructions never left the room. Something else must do the travelling.

"Okay," Eva said. "Watch." She took the chalk. "Say this square is the cell. And this little circle in the middle, that's where the DNA lives. The plans for brown, everything, all in there. Does the DNA come out here to the hair to tell it what to do?"

Daisy considered. "It'd get wrecked. It's the only copy, right? You don't send your only copy out in the rain."

Eva's hand stopped. Something in her chest went quiet and then loud. "Right," she said. "You don't send the original. You make a working copy."

She drew an arrow from the circle toward the edge of the square. On Friday she verified it against the book and found that her guess had the shape of the truth and the details wrong. The cell did make a working copy, and the copy was called messenger RNA. An enzyme did the copying. It was called RNA polymerase, and it read one strand of the DNA, and built a matching strand of messenger RNA to match it, and the messenger RNA carried the gene's instructions out, away from the original, toward whatever needed building. The copy then got read, three letters at a time, and each three-letter group told the cell which amino acid to add next, and the chain of amino acids folded up into a protein, and the protein did the actual work of being brown, or digesting milk, or anything else. Eva wrote none of this down the first time. She just sat with it.

She did write it down, later, in the hayloft, on the back of a feed invoice, in her own words, and then she made Daisy repeat it back, and Daisy, bored, made it a song. "Polymerase, polymerase, reads one strand," Daisy sang, tunelessly, to a cow named Verity, "builds the copy with its hands." The hands part was a travesty of the actual mechanism, and Eva said so, and Daisy sang the verse again, louder, directed now at Eva personally, and the cow swung its head toward them as if to register a complaint.

At the retake on Monday, Eva drew the square and the circle and the arrow in the margin before answering a single question, the way a pianist touches middle C. She filled nine pages. Some of it, she knew when she handed it in, was probably still wrong, probably in the parts about how the code was read, which she could describe but had never quite reconciled with how a cell could possibly know where to start. She was honest on the last page, in a sentence she added and then almost crossed out: that she could follow the process step by step and still could not say she understood it, only that she could now explain it.

She got an eighty-four. She texted Daisy a photograph of the mark, and Daisy texted back a voice note, four seconds long, of the song.
